# PART 8 — PRODUCT IMPLICATIONS

Every recommendation names the findings behind it. Immediate fixes, experiments and research questions are kept separate. These are framed for **a team building a habit product against this incumbent**, which is the decision this analysis informs.

## 8.1 Do not compete on being a better list (§0.1, §5.5, §3.2)

`U_FREE_VALUE` = 902 (3.48%), `PR_ENOUGH` = 645 (2.49%), `PR_SIMPLE` = 1,049 (4.04%) and `PR_BETTER_THAN` = 722 (2.78%) describe an incumbent that is free, pre-installed, Siri-wired, calendar-wired, and *sufficient* for most people. 37 reviewers cancelled paid apps to move **to** it. Inbound switching beats outbound 3.6:1.

**Implication:** a paid product whose pitch is "organise your tasks better" is arguing with a free app that most reviewers already think is good enough. The wedge has to be something Reminders structurally does not do.

## 8.2 The wedge is the record, not the reminder (§0.3, §3.3, §7.6)

`U_HABIT_TRACK_GAP` = 1,163 (4.48%, Very strong), flat for five years, and the mechanism is always the same: **completion destroys the record**. Tick it and it vanishes; miss a day and there is no trace; there is no history, no progress, no streak, no skip.

The specific asks, in order of volume: richer repeat rules (`REQ_FLEXFREQ` 364), usable history (`HAB_NOHIST` 261), visible progress (`REQ_PROGRESS` 180), a resetting daily list (`REQ_RESET` 122), a completion payoff (`REQ_REWARD` 119), an explicit habit mode (`REQ_HABITMODE` 109), skip/pause as distinct from delete (`REQ_PARTIAL` 85), streaks (`REQ_STREAK` 43).

**Implication — build these four first, in this order:**
1. **Repeat-after-completion** and arbitrary intervals. The most-requested and most-cited-when-leaving repeat failure (`14392999764` #24824 documents the oil-change case and names two competitors that do it).
2. **Skip / pause / vacation**, distinct from delete. `12588991225` (#16505) — a medication user forced to delete an entry to skip a dose.
3. **Persistent completion history** with a visible progress view.
4. **A completion payoff** — sound or animation. `REQ_REWARD` sits at 4.38★, i.e. requested by *happy* users; `11628421362` (#11734, 2024-08-19, us, 5★) — "can I get a 'ding' when I complete a task? All the others do this and I need that dopamine hit."

## 8.3 Reliability is the product, not a quality bar (§0.2, §3.5, §4.6)

`U_RELIABILITY` = 6,260 (24.12%) supplies 69.48% of one- and two-star reviews. `NEG_NOTIF_FAIL` is 14.27% of one-star reviews and 0.35% of five-star — a 41× separation, the sharpest in the corpus.

**Implication:** in this category the user has *stopped holding the information themselves* (`DEPEND` = 1,813, 6.99%). A missed notification is not a bug, it is a broken promise, and 248 reviewers express both dependency and breakage in the same review. Notification delivery, sync convergence and never losing data are the entire quality bar. Ship less, but never miss.

## 8.4 Make the alert impossible to ignore — and the permission ask impossible to resent (§0.4, §0.5)

The single feature that converted non-users into users was alarm-strength alerting (`REQ_ALARM` 668, flipping to praise from 2025Q4; `13965378648` #22060 — "prima inutile ora ESSENZIALE"). The single worst three months in the corpus were caused by asking for that feature's permission with a blocking, undismissable prompt.

**Implication:** build persistent, alarm-grade alerting as a first-class mode — `NEG_NOTIF_ONCE` = 326 says the dismissible banner is the core failure. Then ask for the permission **once**, in context, with a real decline path that is remembered. The same capability is a painkiller or a churn event depending entirely on how it is requested.

## 8.5 Never auto-organise without an off switch (§3.7)

Apple Intelligence grocery categorisation is the only net-negative feature in 25,951 reviews (`NEG_GROCERY` 270 + `NEG_APPLEINT` 132 against `PR_APPLEINT` 93), and its negative rate is **rising** quarter on quarter. The single most common sentence is a request for a toggle.

**Implication:** any automatic categorisation, smart sorting or AI assistance ships with a visible, persistent off switch on day one. Also: **it must work in the user's language** — `14470208689` (#25322) reports it working only in English, and this maps onto the storefronts where grocery use is near zero (§6.6).

## 8.6 Target the markets where the gap is loudest, not the biggest market (§6.3, §6.4, §6.5)

The US is 35.44% of the corpus and has a **below-average** habit gap (4.11% vs 4.48%). China is 4.96% of the corpus with a **9.01%** gap — 2.0× global — plus a named, existing behaviour (打卡 check-in) and near-zero engagement with Reminders' flagship grocery feature. India (6.64%), Korea (5.74%) and Japan (5.69%) follow.

**Implication:** US-only user research on this category will systematically understate the opportunity. Weight discovery toward CN, IN, KR, JP.

## 8.7 Cross-platform is the one weakness the incumbent will not fix (§3.11)

`NEG_PLATFORM` = 465 (1.79%) and every instance is structural: no Windows client, a weak web client, no Android, and shared lists that break at the family boundary when one member is not on Apple.

**Implication:** cross-platform presence is a durable differentiator, not a feature. It is also the most common reason in the corpus for an otherwise-happy user to leave.

## 8.8 Pricing: assume resistance, test a one-time purchase (§0.6, §5.4, §5.5)

`MON_WOULD_PAY` = 11 (0.04%). `MON_REFUSE_PAY` = 97 explicitly rejects paying in this category. The one articulate pricing statement rejects ~$100/year and entertains a one-time price.

**Implication:** treat subscription resistance as the default condition. If a subscription is used, it must be justified by something with ongoing cost (sync, cross-platform, coaching), not by feature access. **Test a one-time or lifetime tier** — this is a hypothesis from a single well-argued review (`14522067015` #25682), not a finding, and should be validated with pricing research rather than acted on directly.

## 8.9 Research questions this corpus raises but cannot answer

1. **Does the habit gap convert?** 1,163 reviewers want habit features inside a free app. None of them says they would pay for them elsewhere. Willingness-to-pay must be measured directly.
2. **Is the grocery/habit inversion in China cultural or product-driven?** The corpus shows 打卡 behaviour and near-zero grocery use; it cannot say whether that is because the categoriser is English-first or because the behaviour differs.
3. **What is the real reliability rate?** Everything here is bounded by the +0.87★ non-response gap. Only instrumentation can answer it.
4. **Does a completion payoff change retention, or only satisfaction?** `REQ_REWARD` comes from 4.38★ users — people already happy. It may be a delighter, not a driver.
5. **Would the 465 leave-intent reviewers actually have left?** Review text captures intent at a moment of frustration, not behaviour.

## 8.10 What to copy, and what not to

**Copy:** instant capture (`PR_FAST` 4.92★, the highest mean in the corpus); voice capture that actually files correctly; the satisfaction of checking off (`PR_PROGRESS` 4.90★); shared lists (`PR_SHARED` 4.77★ — loved, and the incumbent's least reliable feature at a 3:2 praise-to-bug ratio); presence on the lock screen and the wrist.

**Do not copy:** completion that destroys the record (§8.2); auto-categorisation without an off switch (§8.5); permission prompts that block the UI (§8.4); an in-app review prompt in mid-task — `SOLICIT` = 142 at a mean of 2.30★, 58.5% of them one-star, costing roughly 0.009★ of corpus mean for nothing (§3.9).

# PART 9 — EVIDENCE APPENDIX

## 9.A Counting rules

1. **Denominator.** Unless a sentence names a narrower scope, every percentage uses **25,951** — all reviews, all 144 storefronts, 2021-09-21 → 2026-09-18.
2. **Non-exclusive themes.** A review may carry any number of codes; mean is 2.43, maximum 11. Code percentages therefore sum to far more than 100%.
3. **Unions count once.** A review carrying `PR_FREE` and `PR_BUILTIN` counts once in `U_FREE_VALUE`.
4. **Segment rates are labelled.** "69.48% of one- and two-star reviews" uses 5,315 as denominator and says so. Segment rates never replace the global signal band.
5. **Mean rating of a code** is the mean star rating of the reviews carrying it. It describes who says a thing, not how good the thing is.
6. **`PR_GENERIC` and `NOISE` carry no interpretive weight.** `PR_GENERIC` (19.44%) is approval with no stated reason; `NOISE` (7.93%) is off-topic, joke or content-free text. Both exist so that the specific codes stay clean.
7. **`HAB_*` codes record behaviour, not intent.** `HAB_DAILY` means the reviewer says they use it daily. It does **not** mean they are building a habit. This is the imposed-lens caveat of §1.6.6, and it is why §0.3 rests on `U_HABIT_TRACK_GAP` (a stated missing capability) rather than on `U_HABIT_ANY`.
8. **Quotes are verbatim.** Every quoted fragment was machine-checked to exist in that review's `title + "\n" + body` after NFKC and curly-quote normalisation. Ellipses mark omitted text; nothing is paraphrased inside quotation marks.
9. **No deduplication was applied.** All 25,951 records are counted, including the 169 that share normalised text with another (§9.H).

## 9.B Taxonomy — all 159 codes

Every code is hand-assigned. `n` is the number of reviews carrying it; `%` uses the 25,951 denominator; mean is the mean star rating of reviews carrying it.

## 9.C Validation, and what it caught

**Per-line validation at write time** (`n1-check-cls.py`, run after every 100-review batch, 260 times): index in range and unique; review ID matches the index; every code defined; no duplicate codes on a line; and **every quoted fragment present verbatim in that review**. Final state: **260 files, 25,951 lines, 0 errors.**

**Errors this caught and that were fixed during coding:**

| Class | Count | Example |
|---|---:|---|
| Undefined code used | ~24 | `PR_CALENDAR_X` → `PR_INTEGRATION`; `SEG_WATCH` → `NEG_PLATFORM`; `HAB_BILLS` → `HAB_CHORE` |
| Duplicate code on one line | 4 | `PR_ORGANISE,PR_PROGRESS,PR_ORGANISE` after a bulk rename |
| Quote not found in review | 5 | #18253 "so easy to keep…" → "easy to keep…"; #20514 "the app has…" → "they app has…"; #19391, #20563, #21992 |
| Unparseable line | 1 | a quote containing a literal newline (#23940) |

**Built-map validation** (`n1-validate.py`), six checks, all passing:

```
corpus            : 25951 reviews, 25951 unique ids
themes            : 159 codes, 63065 assignments
unassigned        : 0
mean codes/review : 2.43
ERRORS            : 0
```

The six checks are: (1) every theme ID exists in `reviews.jsonl`; (2) no intra-theme duplicate IDs; (3) no review assigned to zero themes; (4) `PER_REVIEW` covers every index exactly once with matching IDs; (5) every code defined and no duplicate codes per review; (6) `THEMES` counts reconcile exactly with `PER_REVIEW` counts.

**Report-level validation** (`n1-verify-ids.py`), run after writing: every review ID cited anywhere in this document exists in `reviews.jsonl`, and every `(#index, date, storefront, stars)` shown beside an ID matches the record. Result at §9.M.

**Known residual risk.** Single-coder judgement on adjacent codes, with no inter-rater statistic available. Mitigated by (a) the verbatim-quote anchor, (b) union-level reporting of every headline, (c) the sensitivity re-runs in §9.D.

## 9.D Sensitivity

Every headline re-run with the two distorting windows removed — E1 (the survivorship era, §7.1) and the December 2025–February 2026 regression (§0.5).

| Metric | Full corpus (25,951) | Minus E1 (23,136) | Minus Dec–Feb (24,977) | Minus both (22,162) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Mean rating | 3.940★ | 4.125★ | 3.961★ | 4.156★ |
| `U_PRAISE_ANY` | 56.36% | 60.69% | 56.97% | 61.57% |
| `U_NEG_ANY` | 38.22% | 33.09% | 37.47% | 32.03% |
| `U_RELIABILITY` | 24.12% | 19.71% | 23.45% | 18.76% |
| `U_REQ_ANY` | 20.59% | 19.75% | 20.62% | 19.75% |
| `U_HABIT_ANY` | 18.90% | 19.98% | 18.90% | 20.02% |
| **`U_HABIT_TRACK_GAP`** | **4.48%** | **4.30%** | **4.46%** | **4.26%** |
| `U_FREE_VALUE` | 3.48% | 3.58% | 3.52% | 3.64% |
| `U_SWITCH_ANY` | 5.85% | 5.51% | 5.88% | 5.52% |
| `U_MONEY_ANY` | 1.88% | 1.96% | 1.91% | 2.00% |
| `NEG_UPDATE` | 6.75% | 5.69% | 5.82% | **4.59%** |
| `NEG_NOTIF_FAIL` | 3.27% | **2.04%** | 3.32% | **2.04%** |
| `DEPEND` | 6.99% | 7.08% | 7.01% | 7.12% |
| `PR_GROCERY` | 5.28% | 5.77% | 5.36% | 5.89% |
| `REQ_ALARM` | 2.57% | 2.59% | 2.53% | 2.54% |
| `MON_WOULD_PAY` | 0.04% | 0.03% | 0.04% | 0.03% |

**What changes band:** `NEG_UPDATE` falls from High-priority to Very strong; `NEG_NOTIF_FAIL` falls from Very strong to Meaningful. Both are reliability codes concentrated in the excluded windows, exactly as expected.

**What does not change:** every habit finding, every money finding, every free-value finding, and the direction of every praise code. **`U_HABIT_TRACK_GAP` moves by 0.22 percentage points across all four cuts** — the central finding of this report is insensitive to both distortions.

Both were tightened and re-run; the table shows the tightened results.

**The most consequential row is "habit / routine word" at 0.95% against `U_HABIT_ANY` at 18.90%.** People describe habit behaviour without habit vocabulary — a keyword-first study of this corpus would have concluded the opportunity does not exist.

## 9.G Price points named by reviewers

Only **15 reviews (0.06%)** name a monetary amount at all, and only **9** name one in a pricing context. Every one of those nine:

| Review | Amount | Context |
|---|---|---|
| `8314631565` (#829, 2022-02-03, au, 1★) | 40 dollars | cost of a *missed* reminder — a free trial they failed to cancel |
| `8983501166` (#1520, 2022-08-16, us, 2★) | $60/yr | what they pay a competitor because subtasks were missing |
| `9008163034` (#1553, 2022-08-23, us, 2★) | $1.99, $4 | an upgrade offer in a **different** app, described by mistake |
| `9738483085` (#2291, 2023-03-22, us, 1★) | $1,300 | the price of the phone, cited as an entitlement argument |
| `11356043641` (#10194, 2024-06-08, us, 5★) | $1.00 | distrust of Apple payments generally |
| `11529948809` (#11189, 2024-07-24, us, 1★) | $4 | unrelated |
| `13598623390` (#20476, 2026-01-05, us, 1★) | $237 | unrelated hardware cost |
| `13861415636` (#21440, 2026-03-18, ca, 5★) | $6.99/mo | "Great app that doesn't cost me $6.99 per month! Free is good." |
| `14522067015` (#25682, 2026-09-07, us, 5★) | $100/yr | rejects it; would consider a one-time price |

**Two usable data points in 25,951 reviews: $6.99/month named as the thing avoided, and $100/year named as the thing rejected.** That is not a pricing study, and §8.8 says so.

## 9.H Burst, solicitation and authenticity checks

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| Reviews flagged `is_edited` | **0** of 25,951 |
| Authors appearing more than once | 3 authors, twice each |
| Reviews sharing normalised text with another | **169 (0.65%)** across 49 distinct texts |
| Longest repeated text | **60 characters** — "good good" (23×), "excelente excelente" (9×), "super super" (8×), "好 好" (6×) |
| Repeated texts longer than 60 characters | **0** |
| Referral / promo / giveaway language | **0** |
| Reviews with helpful votes | 1,276 (4.92%) |

**No evidence of astroturfing, review farms, incentivised reviews or copy-paste campaigns.** The 169 duplicates are short generic approval phrases in seven languages — the normal behaviour of people typing the shortest positive thing they can.

**Solicited reviews, however, are measurable and self-inflicted.** `SOLICIT` = 142 (0.55%, mean **2.30★**, 58.5% one-star) are reviews written *about* the in-app review prompt. Distribution by year: 2022 (1), 2023 (18), 2024 (53), 2025 (36), 2026 (34). Removing them would raise the corpus mean from 3.9399★ to 3.9489★ (§3.9).

**Burst behaviour** is real but explained: the December 2025–February 2026 window (§0.5, §7.5) and the September 2023 volume step-change (§7.1). Neither is an authenticity problem; the first is a product regression, the second is a collection artefact.

## 9.I Developer responses

**The schema contains no developer-response field**, so none could be analysed. `NEG_SUPPORT` = 236 (0.91%, 1.88★) records reviewers describing support interactions, and the pattern in those 236 is that contact happened outside the App Store — Apple Support calls, Genius Bar appointments — with **no resolution reported in any of them**. Example: `14464030991` (#25283, 2026-08-23, us, 3★), and `13496927280` (#20236, 2025-12-10, gb, 1★) — "Spoke with Apple support and even went to the Genius Bar."

Every review ID printed anywhere in this document exists in `reviews.jsonl`, and every index, date, storefront and star rating shown beside an ID matches that record exactly.

**What this check caught during writing, and which is disclosed rather than hidden:** the first drafts of Parts 0, 3 and 8 contained **21 review IDs written from memory that did not exist in the corpus**, plus 14 metadata mismatches. All were detected by this verifier, resolved against `reviews.jsonl` by working index, and corrected before the report was finalised. This is why the check exists, and why it is run on the finished text rather than trusted to care during drafting.

**Also verified:** the theme→ID map reconciles exactly with the per-review index (§9.C check 6); the storefront table in §6.2 is generated directly from `reviews.jsonl` and `Tools/native_ratings.json` rather than transcribed; and the corpus totals in §1.3 are reproduced from `manifest.json` and `_state.json` with zero mismatches.
